terms.designer: Realistic textures, lighting and shadows that mimic physical objects. Useful as a metaphor, like a folder or trash can; as full realism it clutters screens and loads slowly.
terms.engineer: Mostly assets, not tokens: textures and objects use the H-motif hook (Q-img-07), custom controls Q-plat-06 custom, and Depth in the shadow-ladder band (56-80).

terms.plain: A strict, tidy grid with plain bold letters lined up on the left and lots of space.
terms.designer: International Typographic Style: a column grid, neo-grotesque type set flush left, big size jumps, asymmetric layouts, neutral colors plus one accent.
terms.engineer: Q-type-03 neo-grotesque, Q-dir-05 start and the flat2 preset, with roundness 0-25 and colorfulness 11-45. The grid itself is layout, not a token.

terms.plain: What we know about how people use apps, made into rules the tool can check.
terms.designer: Laws and heuristics turned into checkable rules: Fitts's law, for example, becomes no target below 24x24 CSS px, applied at the token, component or flow level.
terms.engineer: No DTCG type. Today the rules sit in engine.py: formulas set target floors and contrast; validate checks them. A rule model scoped to token, component or flow is planned.
terms.example: Fitts's law becomes: no tap target smaller than 24 by 24 pixels.

terms.plain: The sneaky tricks the app must never use to push people. A computer can spot some of them.
terms.designer: Which manipulative patterns are banned, and which can be checked automatically: pre-checked consent boxes, unequal accept and reject emphasis, nagging after dismissal, fake countdowns, hard-to-cancel flows.
terms.engineer: No token. Recorded as answers.Q-pattern-05; guardrails.md forbids pre-checked consent. Planned lint would flag pre-checked boxes or cancel flows longer than signup; the rest needs human review.

terms.plain: How much the app works the way people already expect, versus trying new ways of doing things.
terms.designer: How far the product follows platform and industry conventions. Default: conventional behavior with a custom skin; be novel only where it differentiates, test it, and never override standard shortcuts.
terms.engineer: No token. Recorded as answers.Q-plat-10; DESIGN.md keeps navigation, back, sheets and pickers native on every platform. Matches heuristic H4, consistency and standards.

terms.plain: Eight rules of thumb that the top experts agree on, like showing people what is going on.
terms.designer: Eight principles where Nielsen, Norman, Shneiderman, Tognazzini and Laws of UX agree: status and feedback, consistency, error prevention, user control, recognition over recall, plain language, minimalism, expert efficiency.
terms.engineer: Most are partly machine-checkable, such as a dismiss path on every dialog. Today guardrails.md states them as rules for the agent; automated checks are planned.

terms.plain: Making the app work for all kinds of people, like those who are older, see poorly or use one hand.
terms.designer: The accessibility floor, WCAG 2.2 AA by default, plus constraints you design for, such as older users, low vision or one-handed use, which call for larger targets or captions.
terms.engineer: Resolver contexts cover density and reduced motion, not contrast; raw.contrastTarget AAA gives 7:1 text everywhere. CSS follows prefers-reduced-motion and uses rem type for text zoom.

terms.plain: A list of 30 well-known rules about how people use screens, each graded by how strong the proof is.
terms.designer: The 30 laws on lawsofux.com, each graded for evidence. Zeigarnik and choice overload are weak, and Miller's 7 plus or minus 2 does not limit menu length.
terms.engineer: Each law carries an evidence grade: R (research-backed), R- (extrapolated to UI), C (contested), H (heuristic) or P (pop analogy). Showing the grade beside each rule is planned.
terms.designer_says: Laws of UX, graded for evidence
terms.code_name: evidence grade R, R-, C, H, P

terms.plain: How each rule is written down, and if the tool sets it, flags it, or leaves it to a person.
terms.designer: Sets how hard each rule bites: a built-in default, a blocking error, a warning, or human judgment. Some rules, like a seven-item menu cap, must never be automated.
terms.engineer: Planned record: id, principle, evidence grade, scope, check kind, severity, override policy, exceptions. Today validate --json reports each finding as {rule, severity, where, measured, threshold, evidence, fix}.
terms.example: An unlabeled form field would be an error, waived only with a written reason.

terms.plain: How fast the screen must answer you, from a blink that feels instant to a wait that loses you.
terms.designer: How fast the interface must respond, each band with its feedback: acknowledge within 50 ms, no loader under about 1 s, skeletons to 10 s, then progress.
terms.engineer: 16 ms frame, 50 ms acknowledge, 100 ms instant, 200 ms INP, 400 ms Doherty, 1 s, 10 s. Tokens like feedback.acknowledge.max (proposed) = 50ms are not generated.

terms.plain: A set of 72 rules about what makes a screen look clear and well put together.
terms.designer: 72 visual principles, from hierarchy and Gestalt to type pairing and polish, each graded for evidence. The stance: automate strong one-answer principles, make personality ones controls, warn on the rest.
terms.engineer: Catalog P01 to P72, each graded and given a stance: automate, warn or expose as a dial. The engine implements some, such as nested radii and text tiers.

terms.plain: What makes a screen look good: we judge it in a blink, and a middle amount of detail works best.
terms.designer: Research on appeal: judgments form in 17-50 ms, and appeal peaks at moderate complexity and colorfulness. Beauty multiplies usability rather than replacing it, so keep a restrained default.
terms.engineer: Planned, not built: an optional complexity and colorfulness readout from screenshots (the metrics option of answers.Q-pref-01). It is never a usability signal or a pass or fail check.

terms.plain: How things are laid out and lined up on a screen, like on a grid of columns.
terms.designer: The layout model and default alignment. Column grid for app surfaces, hierarchical or bento for marketing; start-aligned everywhere, centered only for single-focus moments with short text.
terms.engineer: Not generated: grid.columns.* (proposed), grid.gutter.* (proposed) and grid.margin.* (proposed); sections use space.section.*. Alignment is a component prop using logical start and end, so RTL mirrors.

terms.plain: How you show that things go together: by space, by boxes around them, or by lines.
terms.designer: Group related items by space, containers or lines; usually a shared boundary beats proximity, which beats similarity. Default: space first, containers when content mixes, lines for long lists.
terms.engineer: space.inset.* and space.stack.* (dimension), color.surface.raised for containers, color.border.subtle with border.width.default for dividers; inner spacing at most half the outer.
terms.designer_says: group by space, containers or lines

terms.plain: How much bigger and bolder the key things look, and how many things may shout at once.
terms.designer: How dramatic contrast between levels is, and how many elements may claim top emphasis. At Expression 50: 1.25 size ratio, three weights, three text colors, one primary action per view.
terms.engineer: Expression sets type.ratio (1.25 at 50) and type.weightCount, feeding font.size.* and font.weight.*; validate warns above three text tiers. A one-primary-per-view lint is planned (spec 6.4).
terms.example: One filled Save button per screen; everything else is quieter.

terms.plain: Tiny fixes that fool the eye into seeing things as even, so the screen feels done.
terms.designer: Optical fixes that make a UI feel finished: optical centering, overshoot, icon optical size, nested radii, one light source. OpenDesigner computes nested radii and icon strokes; optical centering stays manual.
terms.engineer: radius.nested = max(radius.container - space.inset.lg, smallest step), checked by engine.py validate. Icon keylines are guidance; icon.keyline.* (proposed) is not generated.
terms.example: A play icon nudged right so it looks centered in its circle.

terms.plain: How clearly buttons and links show that you can tap or click them.
terms.designer: How clearly clickable things look clickable, via fills, underlines, borders or depth. Default: balanced, with strong signifiers forced for primary actions; minimal only in sparse, conventional layouts.
terms.engineer: Today signifiers use color.bg.action.primary, color.text.link, color.border.input. Planned component tokens: button.primary.background (proposed), link.text-decoration (proposed; no DTCG type), input.border.width (proposed).

terms.plain: The overall look, such as flat, glassy or bold, which sets many small details at once.
terms.designer: An overall style (flat, tonal, glass, soft, neo-brutalist, maximal) that sets shadows, borders and radius together. Recommended: Flat 2.0; with no choice, no preset applies and dials stay at defaults.
terms.engineer: Not a DTCG type: preset (flat2, tonal, glass, neobrutal, soft, maximal) in state.json sets dial positions, which generate shadows, borders and radius.

terms.plain: The basic parts every screen is built from, like color, text, space and shape.
terms.designer: The raw material of every screen: color, type, space, layout, shape, depth, motion, sound, haptics, icons, imagery, data visualization, content, accessibility and input, each a set of scales and roles.
terms.engineer: Each foundation is a family of scales and roles stored as tokens, for example DTCG color, dimension and typography types, that components consume through semantic aliases rather than raw values.
terms.code_name: DTCG color, dimension and typography tokens
terms.example: The same blue and the same 8px gap reused on every screen.

terms.plain: Making the app work for all people, even those who can't see well, can't hear, or can't use a mouse.
terms.designer: Target WCAG 2.2 AA. The system guarantees component behavior and contrast-safe color pairs; product teams own page-level criteria and content. Detailed rules live with each foundation they bound.
terms.engineer: raw.contrastTarget (AA by default, or AAA) sets text minimums; validate checks each listed color pair per theme. Of accessibility settings, only reduced motion is a resolver context today.

terms.plain: The phone settings people pick, like big text or less motion, which the app has to follow.
terms.designer: Honor text size, bold text, increased contrast, reduced transparency, reduced motion, forced colors and screen readers. Never show a boundary or focus state by shadow or translucency alone.
terms.engineer: The resolver's motion modifier (standard, reduced) follows prefers-reduced-motion, and forced-colors maps the focus ring to Highlight. Contrast and transparency modes are not generated yet.
terms.example: With forced colors on, cards keep a border because shadows disappear.

terms.plain: Which colors an app uses, what job each one does, and how they switch for dark mode.
terms.designer: The full color system: how ramps are generated, which roles exist (surface, text, border, status), how light, dark and high-contrast modes remap them, and how contrast is guaranteed.
terms.engineer: Two tiers of DTCG color tokens: primitive ramps (color.accent.light.9) and semantic roles (color.bg.accent.bold) that alias them per theme through the resolver.
terms.example: Blue buttons, gray text and a white page that turns dark at night.

terms.plain: Colors you can partly see through, so they look right on any background.
terms.designer: Semi-transparent fills that adapt to whatever sits beneath, ideal for hover fills, borders and scrims on varied backgrounds. Use solid colors for text, where contrast must be certified.
terms.engineer: A DTCG color value with an alpha field: color.neutral-alpha.light.2 to .12 and dark twins match solid neutral steps over the page; color.overlay.scrim carries alpha too.
terms.example: A light gray hover shade that works on white and on blue.

terms.plain: The one color that makes an app feel like its brand, often on its main button.
terms.designer: Decides how many accents exist and what the brand color does: reserved accent, signature surface or whole fields. Default is neutrals plus one accent; adapt the brand hex for contrast.
terms.engineer: The brand hex, if given, is kept exactly as a seed primitive for logos; UI roles like color.bg.brand alias an accent step, 4.5:1 with color.text.on-brand.
terms.example: The exact logo blue, moved one shade darker so white button text stays readable.

terms.plain: How bold or how soft and calm the colors feel as a whole.
terms.designer: Overall palette saturation, muted to vivid, plus the scheme variant shaping it (Material's TonalSpot, Fidelity or Vibrant). Keep large surfaces calm; spend color on small, meaningful elements.
terms.engineer: No DTCG type of its own: the engine records parameters in opendesigner.meta.json, such as the scheme variant tonalSpot and the accent's HCT chroma, which feed the ramp generator.
terms.example: A calm banking app next to a loud, colorful game.

terms.plain: Text must stand out from what is behind it, and color must never be the only clue.
terms.designer: WCAG 2.2 AA is the floor: 4.5:1 for text, 3:1 for large text and control boundaries. Meaning never depends on color alone; add an icon, label or underline.
terms.engineer: No DTCG contrast field: opendesigner.meta.json lists intended pairs, such as color.text.primary on color.surface.base at 4.5:1, and engine.py validate checks each per theme.
terms.designer_says: WCAG AA contrast, never color alone
terms.example: An error field shows a red border plus an icon and message, not red alone.

terms.plain: Bold color blends for ads and pictures, kept off buttons and forms.
terms.designer: Brand gradients and campaign colors that live outside core controls, on marketing and illustration surfaces. Keep them off interactive components; if a gradient carries data meaning, use a sequential palette.
terms.engineer: DTCG 2025.10 gradient type: an array of stops, each with color and position. It has no kind, angle or interpolation space, so store those in $extensions; interpolate in OKLab.
terms.example: A purple-to-orange blend on a sale banner, never on the checkout button.

terms.plain: Full swaps of an app's colors, like light, dark, or a sharper set that is easier to see.
terms.designer: The alternative color mappings a system ships: light, dark, dimmed, high contrast and colorblind-safe, and how each platform picks one. Dark mode is a separate mapping, never an inversion.
terms.engineer: The DTCG Resolver module's theme modifier: light and dark contexts point semantic tokens at different files. Web CSS uses prefers-color-scheme with a [data-theme] override.
terms.example: Your phone switches to dark at night and the app follows.

terms.term: Appearance modes by platform and device
terms.plain: Which light or dark looks each kind of device uses, and who gets to switch between them.
terms.designer: Which appearances each device class gets and who switches: system setting, in-app override or ambient light. Phones and desktops follow the system; watches stay dark; cars switch day and night.
terms.engineer: sketch --theme (system-light-dark, light-dark-toggle, light-only, dark-only) sets which theme contexts exist; web CSS adds a [data-theme] override. Per-device availability, such as wrist dark only, is not generated yet.
terms.designer_says: appearance by device: system or override
terms.example: A watch app that is always dark, even at noon.

terms.plain: Extra color sets for people who need text to stand out more, or who mix up colors.
terms.designer: Themes for users who need more contrast or hue separation: contrast levels, high contrast, forced colors, colorblind-safe palettes. Back fills with borders or icons so they survive forced colors.
terms.engineer: Not generated yet: extra resolver modifiers beside theme, such as contrast (standard, high) and vision (protan-deutan, tritan). Material offers three contrast levels; web forced-colors mode swaps in system colors.
terms.example: Primer's colorblind theme shows success in blue instead of green.

terms.plain: How each color is picked again for dark screens, so text stays easy to read.
terms.designer: Each role gets its own dark value, mapped by role, not flipped. The default dark base is neutral step 2, untinted at Warmth 50; accents go lighter.
terms.engineer: Semantic tokens resolve per Resolver context (light, dark); each role takes the dark step giving the same contrast relationship as in light. Web: prefers-color-scheme with a [data-theme] override.
terms.example: White text on a near-black page, with the blue lightened a step.

terms.plain: The set of grays, from white to near black, used for most backgrounds, lines and text.
terms.designer: The gray scale behind most surfaces, borders and text. A slight tint toward the accent hue feels branded; pure gray suits image and data tools.
terms.engineer: Primitives color.neutral.light.1 to .12 and a dark twin, tinted by the Warmth dial, plus alpha twins color.neutral-alpha.light.2 to .12. Semantic roles alias them.
terms.example: Near-white for the page, mid gray for borders, dark gray for text.

terms.plain: Whether an app can take on colors you pick, like your wallpaper, or keeps its own.
terms.designer: Whether the OS or user may recolor the product (Android wallpaper-based dynamic color, macOS accent, Apple icon looks) or keeps a fixed brand palette. Keep brand-critical and status colors fixed.
terms.engineer: Dynamic roles resolve at runtime, so tokens store roles plus the generator recipe (source, variant, spec version, contrast level). Android applies it via DynamicColors; brand tokens remain the fallback.
terms.designer_says: dynamic color or fixed brand palette
terms.example: A notes app turns green because your wallpaper is a forest.

terms.plain: A row of shades of one color, from light to dark, where each step has a job.
terms.designer: What a step promises differs by system: Tailwind lightness varies by hue, Spectrum keeps equal contrast per step, Material uses HCT tone. Radix gives each step a job.
terms.engineer: Primitive color tokens per ramp and theme, such as color.accent.light.1 to .12: 12 contrast-indexed steps generated in OKLCH from a seed color.
terms.example: Pale blue for a background, deep blue for the text on it.

terms.plain: Color names that say the job, like page background or warning text, not the shade.
terms.designer: Named jobs such as background, text, border and icon, crossed with roles like accent, neutral or danger and emphasis levels (subtle, default, bold). Components use roles, never raw values.
terms.engineer: Semantic tier named property, role, emphasis, state: color.bg.accent.bold aliases {color.accent.light.9}, with .bold-hover and .bold-pressed. Bold fills pair with on-colors such as color.text.on-accent.
terms.designer_says: color roles by job and emphasis
terms.example: Change the danger color once and every error message updates.

terms.plain: Colors for lines around things, and for the ring that shows where the keyboard is.
terms.designer: Subtle, default and strong border strengths plus one focus color per mode. Interactive borders and focus rings need 3:1 against adjacent colors; decorative dividers do not.
terms.engineer: color.border.subtle (dividers), .default, .strong, .input, .focus (the focus ring), .accent and one per status. In forced-colors mode browsers replace border and outline colors with system colors.
terms.example: A soft gray line between list rows, a blue ring on the active field.

terms.plain: Colors for words and icons, from strong main text to faint hint text.
terms.designer: Text and icon colors by emphasis: primary, secondary, placeholder, disabled and inverse, plus an on-color for each bold fill. Secondary text should still pass 4.5:1 on its lowest surface.
terms.engineer: Solid semantic tokens color.text.{primary|secondary|tertiary|disabled|inverse|on-brand} and color.icon.*, aliasing ramp steps per mode. WCAG requires 4.5:1 for normal text; disabled text is exempt.
terms.designer_says: text and icon colors by emphasis
terms.example: Black for headings, gray for hints, white text on a blue button.

terms.plain: Colors that show how things went, like green for success and red for an error.
terms.designer: Success, warning, danger and info, each subtle and bold, for fills, text and icons. Always pair with an icon or words; yellow fills need dark text.
terms.engineer: color.bg.success.subtle, .bold and .bold-hover, color.text.success, color.border.success and color.text.on-success; the same for warning, danger, info. Status icons take the text token.
terms.example: A green check beside 'Saved', a red icon beside 'Payment failed'.

terms.plain: Background colors for things that stack, like a page, a card on it, and a pop-up on top.
terms.designer: Background tiers (base, raised, overlay, sunken) that show layering. In light mode, shadow or border plus a subtle tone separates them; in dark mode, lighter tones do.
terms.engineer: color.surface.base, .raised, .sunken, .overlay and .nav, plus .tinted at Colorfulness 50 and up, aliasing neutral or accent steps with separate light and dark values.
terms.example: A white card sitting on a light gray page.

terms.plain: How colors are mixed so each step looks even, and how bold a screen's colors can get.
terms.designer: Perceptual spaces such as OKLCH or HCT make equal steps look equally heavy across hues, so hierarchy survives color swaps. Gamut decides whether vivid Display P3 accents are allowed.
terms.engineer: DTCG color values set colorSpace ('oklch', 'srgb', 'display-p3') with a hex fallback. OpenDesigner writes OKLCH ramps with hex fallbacks and P3 variants in $extensions.opendesigner.p3.
terms.example: Blue and green buttons at the same step look equally strong.

terms.plain: How a button's color shifts when you point at it, press it, pick it, or can't use it.
terms.designer: Hover, pressed, selected and disabled colors come from stepping along the ramp; a translucent state layer covers colors unknown at design time. Selected needs a non-color cue.
terms.engineer: Ramp steps per role, such as color.bg.accent.bold-hover (+1 step) and .bold-pressed (+2), and state-layer numbers such as opacity.state.hover = 0.08 for colors unknown at design time.
terms.example: A blue button turns one shade darker under the mouse.

terms.plain: The words in the app and the rules for writing them, so the app always sounds like itself.
terms.designer: The words layer: voice, tone by situation, mechanics, component microcopy, terminology, localization, readability and scannable structure. Voice stays the same across platforms; platform feature terms adapt.
terms.engineer: No DTCG type: content rules are text records; lint settings such as content.readingGrade.max (proposed) are not built yet. DESIGN.md has a Content and Voice section.

terms.plain: Rules so the app works in other languages, where words get longer or go right to left.
terms.designer: Never fix a label width to English length; budget 2-3x for labels under 10 characters. Plan right-to-left layouts, per-script line heights and local date and number formats early.
terms.engineer: CSS export scales line height per listed script via :lang(); per-script font.family modes are not generated. Use CLDR locale formatting and test the brand face against OS fallbacks.
terms.example: A short English label may need three times the room once translated.

terms.plain: House rules for writing, like when to use capitals, how to write dates, and when to say you.
terms.designer: Sentence case everywhere; contractions yes, except negative ones in high-stakes flows; you for the user, we sparingly; no exclamation marks in errors; numerals for counts.
terms.engineer: No DTCG type, and the typography composite has no text-transform, so casing stays a content rule. Dates and numbers go through CLDR-based locale formatters, never hard-coded formats.
terms.example: Save changes, not Save Changes.

terms.plain: The short bits of text that come with each part, like button words and error notes.
terms.designer: Each component spec ships its wording rules with examples: verb-first button labels, useful empty states, constructive errors and confirmations that name the action.
terms.engineer: Default strings would be i18n keys such as button.submit.label (proposed), not design tokens; none are generated yet. Platform labels (Cancel, OK, Done) follow OS conventions.
terms.example: The delete dialog's button says Delete file, not OK.

terms.plain: Keeping the words short and plain so that most people can read them fast.
terms.designer: Aim for grade 6-8 reading level in consumer products and 10-12 in expert tools. Button labels are 2-4 words, verb first. Plain language helps everyone, experts included.
terms.engineer: Proposed lint, not built: content.readingGrade.max (proposed) and button.label.maxWords (proposed) = 4. Spec 6.4 plans a warning for button labels over 4 words; no string lint exists yet.
terms.example: Save draft, not Persist current document state.

terms.plain: Laying out words so people can skim: clear headings, the main point first, and lists instead of long blocks.
terms.designer: A heading for every section, key points in the first two paragraphs, sparing bold, bullets for three or more items. Unformatted walls of text push readers into the F-pattern.
terms.engineer: Real heading structure (WCAG 1.3.1, 2.4.6) using type role tokens. Linting for skipped heading levels, long unheaded paragraphs and link text like click here is not built yet.
terms.example: A help page where each heading answers one question.

terms.plain: A shared word list: words to use, words to avoid, and kind ways to talk about people.
terms.designer: A glossary of preferred and banned terms plus inclusive-language rules, started at 20-50 terms on day one. Consistent terms make navigation labels, headings and empty states predictable.
terms.engineer: Glossary data, not tokens: a term list. Linting copy against it for banned terms and internal jargon is not built yet. Shared strings avoid input-specific verbs like tap or click.
terms.example: Pick sign in and use it everywhere, never mixed with log in.

terms.plain: How the app's words change with the moment: calm for mistakes, warmer for good news.
terms.designer: Voice stays; tone shifts by message type. Errors are serious, respectful and matter-of-fact; success is as warm as the brand allows; humor is rare, since repeated jokes annoy.
terms.engineer: Not tokens: a matrix of message type against humor, formality, enthusiasm and length, kept as a content rule. Notification and lock-screen strings get tighter, context-aware limits.
terms.example: Payment failed: plain and calm. Payment sent: a little warmth.

terms.plain: The way the app sounds in words, the same each time, like a friend you know by their voice.
terms.designer: The brand's lasting personality in words, set as 3-4 traits, each with a but-not and three copy examples, such as authoritative but not pedantic. Tone flexes; voice stays.
terms.engineer: Not a design token: traits, anti-traits and examples belong in a voice guide (hook H-voice). DESIGN.md's Content and Voice section records the guidance level, casing and contractions.
terms.code_name: voice guide (H-voice), DESIGN.md Content and Voice
terms.example: Practical, but not dull, with three sample lines for each trait.

terms.plain: Charts that match the rest of the app, with set colors, parts and rules so all can read them.
terms.designer: Charts as part of the system: a small set of chart types, palettes, shared anatomy and accessibility rules, so charts look native to the product rather than pasted in.
terms.engineer: Generated when Q-color-19 asks for chart colors: color.chart.* holds brand, categorical, sequential, diverging and status colors, each 3:1 on the page, plus axis, gridline and label aliases.
terms.designer_says: data viz, themed to the system

terms.plain: Making charts clear to people who can't tell some colors apart or who have the screen read aloud.
terms.designer: Every chart gets a title stating the insight, direct labels or a legend with shape cues, a text summary and a view-as-table option. Color is never the only cue.
terms.engineer: Meets WCAG 1.4.1 and 1.4.11 (3:1 for essential marks). Long descriptions via figure and figcaption or aria-describedby, a data table alternative, and patterns or markers as assets.
terms.example: Title: Sales doubled in March, with a table view below.

terms.plain: The parts of a chart, like its grid lines, labels, color key and pop-up notes, and how each looks.
terms.designer: Axes, gridlines, labels, legends and tooltips reuse the UI's text and border styles to match the product. Faint gridlines keep focus on data; direct labels read cleaner than legends.
terms.engineer: Not generated yet: component aliases such as chart.gridline.color (proposed) = {color.border.subtle} and chart.tick.label.color (proposed) = {color.text.secondary}; chart-only tokens just for marks and states.
terms.example: Grid lines use the same faint grey as table borders.

terms.plain: Chart colors: one per group, light to dark for how much, and two-way for above or below the middle.
terms.designer: One brand chart color plus grey by default; 6-8 categorical colors in fixed order for neighbor contrast; one sequential ramp per primary hue and one diverging ramp, per mode.
terms.engineer: Not generated yet: per-mode color tokens color.chart.categorical.1 (proposed) onward, color.chart.sequential (proposed) and color.chart.diverging (proposed) ramps, plus brand, neutral and status sets.
terms.example: This year in brand blue, last year in grey for context.

terms.plain: Which kinds of charts the app has, like bars and lines, and which ready-made chart kit it styles.
terms.designer: Start with 5-6 types (bar, line, area, stacked bar, donut or meter, scatter) plus a KPI big number. Fewer types stay consistent; theme a library rather than build one.
terms.engineer: Not a token: the Q-viz-01 scope answer in state.json. The themed chart library would consume color.chart.* (proposed) and existing chrome tokens, as would native chart frameworks.
terms.example: A dashboard with bars, lines and one big number, all from one library.

terms.plain: How the app shows that some parts sit on top of others, with shadows, shades and glass.
terms.designer: The depth family: depth model, levels, shadow recipe, surface tiers, stacking order, translucent materials, and opacity for states and scrims. Together they decide what looks flat and what floats.
terms.engineer: DTCG shadow composites (color, offsetX, offsetY, blur, spread, inset), surface color tokens and opacity number tokens; layer order is not tokenized yet. Blur and materials have no DTCG type.
terms.code_name: DTCG shadow, surface and opacity tokens

terms.plain: The main way the app shows layers: with lines, shadows, shades of color, or frosted glass.
terms.designer: Pick flat with borders, shadows, tonal steps or translucent material. OpenDesigner's default (Depth 40) is tonal: surface steps for in-page containers, shadows only for floating menus and dialogs.
terms.engineer: The Depth dial picks a model (borders, ring+faint-shadow, tonal, shadow-ladder, materials), stored in the elevation group's $extensions.opendesigner.model; it decides which shadow and surface tokens are emitted.
terms.example: GOV.UK uses borders only; Material uses tonal color steps.

terms.plain: See-through frosted glass on bars and menus, with a solid look for people who turn it off.
terms.designer: Glass, blur and vibrancy feel premium and keep context visible but cut contrast. Use them only for floating navigation and overlays, never reading surfaces; each needs an opaque fallback.
terms.engineer: No DTCG material type. The materials depth model adds material.glass.blur, a glass surface color and a solid fallback for reduced transparency. Web: backdrop-filter; iOS: glassEffect; Windows: Mica, Acrylic.
terms.example: A frosted tab bar turns solid when Reduce Transparency is on.

terms.plain: A faint tint when you press, a faded look for things you can't use, and a dim veil behind pop-ups.
terms.designer: Material's state layers: 0.08 hover, 0.10 focus and press, 0.16 drag, 0.38 disabled. OpenDesigner steps the ramp first and uses these only for unknown colors. Scrims dim pages behind modals.
terms.engineer: DTCG number tokens (0-1): opacity.state.hover, opacity.disabled.content. Scrim: color.overlay.scrim, a color with alpha, 40-50% in light mode and 50-60% in dark.
terms.example: A dialog opens over the page, which dims behind a dark veil.

terms.plain: How many heights a part can sit at above the page, and which parts go at each one.
terms.designer: Four levels (sunken, default, raised, overlay) cover most products; more levels muddy the order. Two parts at the same level should never overlap each other.
terms.engineer: Semantic shadow tokens elevation.raised, .floating and .overlay. The shadow-ladder and materials models alias a six-step primitive ladder; the tonal default writes its shadows inline.
terms.example: Code wells sunken, pages default, hover cards raised, dialogs overlay.

terms.plain: Rules for shadows: how many, how soft, what color, and how they change on dark screens.
terms.designer: Two layers: 1px contact shadow plus a soft blur growing with height, neutral at 8-24% alpha. Dark mode doubles alpha and adds a 1px edge ring.
terms.engineer: A DTCG shadow array of layers {color, offsetX, offsetY, blur, spread, inset}. Colors reference color.shadow.key and color.shadow.ambient so dark mode swaps them; Figma stores effect styles.
terms.example: A menu gets a thin edge shadow plus a wide, soft blur.

terms.plain: A set order for what goes on top when things pile up, so pop-ups never hide.
terms.designer: A named layer order: base, sticky, dropdown, scrim, modal, popover or tooltip, toast, skip link. It keeps tooltips above modals and toasts above everything.
terms.engineer: Not generated yet: number tokens like layer.modal (proposed), named by role, spaced by 100. Avoid hard-coded z-index; the web top layer (popover, dialog) cuts the need.
terms.example: A tooltip opened inside a dialog still shows on top.

terms.plain: The set of background shades for each layer, where higher layers get a bit lighter on dark screens.
terms.designer: Four surface tiers (sunken, default, raised, overlay). In dark mode each higher tier is 3-5% lighter, as if lit from the front, because shadows barely show on dark backgrounds.
terms.engineer: Role-named color tokens color.surface.sunken, .base, .raised, .overlay and .nav, with light and dark values. Shadows are separate elevation.* tokens; the same tiers appear under Surface roles.
terms.designer_says: surface tiers, lighter in dark mode
terms.example: In dark mode a menu sits on a slightly lighter grey than the page.

terms.plain: Small signs for actions and things, like a trash can for delete, and the rules for how they look.
terms.designer: The UI icon system: source, style, construction, sizes, states, color, labels, naming, larger tiers, delivery and platform symbols. Consistent icons make rows look even and actions easy to recognize.
terms.engineer: No DTCG icon type: glyphs are SVG assets, with custom ones from hook H-icons (a manifest is proposed); size.icon.*, icon.stroke.* and color.icon.* are tokens.

terms.plain: The colors icons use: mostly one calm grey, with bright colors saved for warnings and errors.
terms.designer: One neutral icon color matched to secondary text, status colors only on status icons, no decorative multicolor. Meaningful icons need 3:1 (WCAG); Carbon asks 4.5:1 beside body text.
terms.engineer: color.icon.default (same neutral step as color.text.secondary, not an alias), .subtle, .accent and .on-accent; status icons use color.text.danger and its siblings. Web SVG: fill=currentColor.
terms.example: Grey icons in the toolbar, and a red one only beside an error.

terms.plain: Drawing rules for icons, like line width and a shared grid, so they all look the same size.
terms.designer: Stroke matches text weight: about 1.5px by 14-16px text, 2px at 24px. Material's 24px grid, 20px live area and keylines keep icons even.
terms.engineer: Mostly documented, not tokenized. The engine emits icon.stroke.sm, .md and .lg (dimension) from round_to_0.5((size/12) x (weight/400)), minimum 1. Glyphs themselves are SVG assets.
terms.example: A 24px icon with a 2px line inside a 20px live area.

terms.plain: How icon files are packed and sent to each kind of app, like phone apps and websites.
terms.designer: One SVG master feeds every platform package, so icons match everywhere. Files are named by name, size and style; size and color come from the system, not the artwork.
terms.engineer: SVG source of truth generates framework components, Android vector drawables and iOS PDF, SVG or custom SF Symbols; web uses inline SVG with fill=currentColor. Files follow <name>_<size>_<style>.
terms.designer_says: one SVG master for every platform
terms.example: home_24_filled.svg becomes a React component and an Android drawable.

terms.plain: When an icon needs words beside it, and how the icon and the words line up.
terms.designer: Label everything in navigation. Icon-only suits about a dozen universal actions (search, close, more, add, delete, edit, share, settings), each with a tooltip. Center icons on the text line.
terms.engineer: space.icon.gap (proposed), 4px at 16px icons, is not generated; use space.inline.xs or .sm. Icon-only controls need an accessible name; decorative icons get aria-hidden.
terms.example: A bare magnifier for search, while Settings in the sidebar keeps its label.

terms.plain: How icons get names, what each one means, and which ones flip for writing that goes right to left.
terms.designer: Name icons by shape (shield, not security) so one glyph serves many meanings, add function aliases in the component API, note mirroring per icon, test metaphors per market.
terms.engineer: Proposed, not generated yet: an icon manifest in JSON with name, aliases, directionType (unique or mirror, as Fluent does) and categories per icon. Components expose the function-alias layer.
terms.designer_says: name icons by shape, not meaning
terms.example: The back arrow points right in Arabic and Hebrew layouts.

terms.plain: Using the phone's own icons for common jobs like share and back, and the brand's icons for the rest.
terms.designer: Use platform-standard glyphs for system actions (share, back, close, more, search, settings), since people know their own platform's version. The brand set covers product-specific ideas.
terms.engineer: A semantic icon maps to per-platform assets, such as icon.share (proposed) = {ios: square.and.arrow.up, android: a Material name, web: an SVG}; no icon map is generated yet.
terms.example: Share shows Apple's box-and-arrow on iPhone and the Android share glyph elsewhere.

terms.plain: A few set icon sizes, each one matched to the size of the words next to it.
terms.designer: Ship 16, 20 and 24px (12 and 32 if needed), each paired to the adjacent text's line height: 16 with 14px text, 20 with 16, 24 with 20.
terms.engineer: Dimension tokens size.icon.sm (16), .md (20) and .lg (24), plus size.icon.default set by the Density dial. Material Symbols add an optical-size axis from 20 to 48.
terms.example: A 16px icon sits beside 14px body text in a list row.

terms.plain: Whether to use a ready-made set of icons, add to one, or draw your own from scratch.
terms.designer: Native sets feel at home, open-source sets look neutral, custom sets carry the most brand but cost the most. Default: native on apps, one open-source set on web.
terms.engineer: A system setting, not a token: icon.library (proposed) would name sf-symbols, material-symbols-rounded, lucide or custom. Custom additions use the library's own template so stroke, radius and keylines match.
terms.example: SF Symbols on iPhone, one open-source set on the web.

terms.plain: How an icon changes when you pick it, press it, or can't use it.
terms.designer: Outline at rest, filled plus accent color when selected: two cues, so it still works for color-blind people. Hover and pressed feedback go on the container, not the glyph.
terms.engineer: Not generated yet: icon.fill.selected (proposed) = 1 and icon.grade.emphasis (proposed) = 200 for variable-font axes. Color is generated: color.icon.default at rest, color.icon.accent when selected.
terms.designer_says: outline at rest, filled plus accent
terms.example: The active tab icon is filled and blue; the rest are grey outlines.

terms.plain: Whether icons are drawn as lines or filled in, with round or sharp corners, to fit the brand.
terms.designer: Outlined at rest, filled when selected. Match corners to the radius family (rounded icons with pill buttons, sharp icons with 0-2px corners) and stroke to body text weight.
terms.engineer: Not tokens: the rest style, outline by default, is a param in opendesigner.meta.json. With Material Symbols, icon.fill.selected (proposed) = 1 would drive the FILL axis.
terms.designer_says: outlined at rest, filled when selected
terms.example: A home tab icon is an outline, then fills in when tapped.

terms.plain: Big icons with more detail for welcome screens and ads, in the same style as the small ones.
terms.designer: Pictograms and spot icons bridge UI icons and full illustration in feature grids and onboarding. Add them only with marketing surfaces, drawn with the UI icon's stroke logic scaled up.
terms.engineer: Not generated yet: larger dimension tokens such as icon.size.pictogram (proposed) = 64px and icon.size.spot (proposed) = 120px. The drawings are SVG assets beside the UI set.
terms.example: A 64px pictogram above each item in a feature grid.

terms.plain: Rules for the photos, drawings, logo and app icon you see in the app.
terms.designer: The picture layer: photo direction, aspect ratios, text on images, loading, illustration, rich media, graphic motifs and brand marks. It sets mood and brand without competing with content.
terms.engineer: No DTCG type for images or aspect ratios. An asset manifest (proposed) would list files for components; none is generated. Of the related tokens, only color.overlay.scrim exists today.

terms.plain: The app's icon on your home screen, its logo inside, and the tiny icon on a web page tab.
terms.designer: App icon: 1-3 filled shapes, checked in tinted and monochrome first. In product, a 24-32px symbol-only logo in the app bar; the full lockup on sign-in.
terms.engineer: Assets, not tokens: Apple layered icons, Android adaptive foreground, background and monochrome layers, a maskable PWA icon, and favicons from one SVG master (an SVG favicon plus favicon.ico).
terms.example: A 32px symbol in the app bar, the full wordmark on sign-in.

terms.plain: How the app's drawings look, and where they show up, like on an empty page or a welcome screen.
terms.designer: One style drawn from icon stroke, radius and palette, used in empty, error, success and onboarding states. Neutral spots for routine states, colorful for first run; little humor in errors.
terms.engineer: Mostly guidance; no illustration tokens are generated yet: illustration.color.* (proposed) aliasing brand primitives, illustration.stroke.width (proposed), illustration.size.spot (proposed). Drawings come through the H-illus hook.
terms.example: A calm grey drawing on an empty inbox, a colorful one after sign-up.

terms.plain: What you see while a picture is still loading or fails to load, so the page does not jump.
terms.designer: Always reserve the final box so layout stays still. Use a neutral placeholder fill for images, skeletons only for container components, and a fallback image when the source fails.
terms.engineer: Reserve space with width and height or CSS aspect-ratio so CLS stays at or below 0.1 for 75% of visits. Placeholder fill: a color token; pulse: duration.skeleton.pulse (proposed).
terms.example: A grey box the size of the photo holds its place until it loads.

terms.plain: Shapes and patterns that belong to the brand, used here and there to make the app feel like its own.
terms.designer: Signature shapes, patterns, crops, frames and gradients from the brand identity. Use them only on expressive surfaces (marketing, onboarding, empty states, hero moments) so they never compete with content.
terms.engineer: SVG assets referenced by component props rather than tokens; gradients can be DTCG gradient tokens. On Apple platforms, brand content belongs on onboarding, not the launch screen.
terms.example: Dropbox's diamond shapes on a welcome screen, not in file lists.

terms.plain: Rules for which photos to use: who is in them, the angle, the light, and the colors.
terms.designer: A one-paragraph brief (subjects, perspective, light, color treatment, casting) written before shooting or buying stock. Natural light reads factual; warm, graded color reads aspirational.
terms.engineer: Mostly guidance, not tokens. A color treatment would become image.overlay.color (proposed) and image.overlay.opacity (proposed). Apple platforms take JPEG or HEIC with an embedded color profile.
terms.example: Real customers at eye level in natural light, with ungraded color.

terms.plain: A short list of photo shapes, like wide or square, and where on the screen each one goes.
terms.designer: Allow 3-5 ratios (16:9, 3:2, 4:3, 1:1, optionally 2:1), one per component slot. A small set keeps grids calm; wide feels cinematic, square product-focused.
terms.engineer: No DTCG ratio type: store a number (aspect.video (proposed) = 1.7778) or a 16 / 9 string in $extensions for CSS aspect-ratio. iOS bitmaps need @2x and @3x.
terms.example: 16:9 for heroes, 4:3 for card media, 1:1 for avatars.

terms.plain: Moving icons, emoji and 3D art, kept for big moments like a first visit.
terms.designer: Animate icons only to confirm an action or show ongoing status. Keep 3D and Lottie for onboarding, celebration and marketing; they feel alive but are heavy and can distract.
terms.engineer: Timing uses motion tokens (duration, cubicBezier) and obeys reduced motion; the files themselves are assets, not tokens. dotLottie v2.0 packs animations, themes and state machines into one file.
terms.example: A checkmark that draws itself once when an upload finishes.

terms.plain: Ways to keep words easy to read when they sit on a photo, like a dark fade behind them.
terms.designer: Put text beside images by default. When a hero needs text on top, add a scrim or protection gradient and test contrast against the image's worst-case region.
terms.engineer: Scrim tokens: color.overlay.scrim (color with alpha), or gradient.scrim.bottom (proposed). Text must keep 4.5:1, or 3:1 when large, over the lightest region behind it.
terms.example: A white headline on a beach photo gets a dark fade at the bottom.

terms.plain: All the ways people control an app, like touch, mouse, keyboard, TV remote or voice.
terms.designer: The inputs the system supports (touch, pointer, keyboard, remote, gaze, voice, rotary) and what depends on them: target sizes, target spacing and focus. These follow input precision, not device.
terms.engineer: Dimension tokens for target size and spacing (size.target.min, space.target.gap) plus focus-ring tokens, keyed to input mode such as pointer, touch or remote rather than device type.
terms.example: A laptop with a touchscreen gets finger-sized targets on its touch surfaces.

terms.plain: The outline that shows where you are when you move with the keyboard or a TV remote.
terms.designer: The visible ring showing keyboard, remote or switch focus. Default: 2px solid ring at 2px offset, following the component's radius, with 3:1 contrast against every surface.
terms.engineer: focus.ring.width and focus.ring.offset (dimension), color.border.focus (color) and radius.focus (control radius + offset); DTCG has no outline type. Web: :focus-visible with outline and outline-offset.
terms.example: Pressing Tab puts a ring around the next link.

terms.plain: Which ways of using the app each screen must handle, like tap, click or type.
terms.designer: Which inputs each surface must support, and how density and targets switch between them. Default: touch-size targets on mobile and web, a pointer density mode for desktop.
terms.engineer: size.target.min matches the main input, from size.target.pointer or .touch. Floors: 44 iOS, 48 Android, 24 or 44 web, 28 macOS, 66 tvOS, 60 visionOS.
terms.example: A web app uses 44px targets for touch, even though 24px passes.

terms.plain: How big and how far apart buttons must be so fingers don't hit the wrong one.
terms.designer: Minimum hit area and target spacing by input precision: pointer 24px, finger 44-48, remote and gaze 56-66. Visuals may shrink with density; hit areas never do.
terms.engineer: Fixed tokens: size.target.min (24px web AA floor, 44pt iOS, 48dp Android) and space.target.gap (8 pointer, 12 touch). Web detects via pointer: coarse | fine.
terms.designer_says: minimum hit area and target spacing
terms.example: A small close icon still gets a 44-point tap area on iPhone.

terms.plain: How a screen is split into areas, and how those areas move when the screen size changes.
terms.designer: How screens divide and adapt: breakpoints, column grids, containers and maximum widths, reflowing and switching layouts, and safe areas. App shells and canonical layouts live with patterns.
terms.engineer: Not generated yet: dimension and number tokens for grids, margins and max widths. DTCG has no breakpoint or media-condition type, so breakpoints compile to build-time variables or resolver contexts.
terms.example: One column on a phone, a sidebar and content on a laptop.

terms.plain: How a layout fits different screen sizes, by stretching or by changing to a new layout.
terms.designer: Responsive means reflowing within a layout; adaptive means switching layouts at breakpoints, such as pane count or navigation type. Default: responsive inside panes, adaptive between breakpoints.
terms.engineer: Page layout uses viewport media queries; components use CSS container queries, with sizes like container.sm (proposed) = 24rem. Variant switching lives in code, not tokens.
terms.example: A list becomes a list plus detail view on a wide tablet.

terms.plain: The window widths where the layout switches, like when a phone view turns into a tablet view.
terms.designer: Window widths where the layout changes. Adopt Material's five width breakpoints for cross-platform work or Tailwind's set for web-only; design mobile first, then reveal, divide, resize, reposition or swap.
terms.engineer: Dimension tokens such as breakpoint.md (proposed) = 48rem are not generated yet. Media queries cannot read custom properties, so compile at build time. Android: WindowSizeClass; iOS: size classes.
terms.example: At 48rem the single column splits into two.

terms.plain: How wide the main content may get, so lines of text don't stretch across a huge screen.
terms.designer: How content is framed: centered reading columns (max about 1280px, text 40-80 characters), navigation plus left-aligned content, or fluid data surfaces. Ask: reading, working or monitoring?
terms.engineer: A dimension token, layout.container.max (proposed) = 80rem, not generated yet. 65ch is not a valid DTCG dimension (px or rem only), so keep it in CSS.
terms.designer_says: max content width and reading column
terms.example: A blog post stays in a centered column even on a wide monitor.

terms.plain: Hidden columns that line things up on a page, like the lines on graph paper.
terms.designer: Columns, gutters and margins: 4, 8 or 12 columns as width grows, 16-24px gutters, 16px margins on compact, 24px above. Type never hangs into the gutter.
terms.engineer: Not generated yet: grid.columns.* (proposed) as number tokens, grid.gutter.* and grid.margin.* (proposed) as dimensions, one value per breakpoint. Native mobile uses panes and layout guides.
terms.example: Cards spanning 4 of 12 columns, three to a row.

terms.term: Safe areas, insets and edge policy
terms.plain: Keeping buttons and text away from notches, screen edges and folds where they get cut off.
terms.designer: Backgrounds run edge to edge; interactive content stays inside the safe area, clear of notches, system bars and hinges. TVs keep the outer 5% clear.
terms.engineer: Insets are runtime values from the platform, not tokens; tokens add padding on top, such as layout.safe.extra (proposed) = 16. Web needs viewport-fit=cover plus env(safe-area-inset-*).
terms.example: A video fills the whole screen, but its buttons stay clear of the notch.

terms.plain: How things in the app move: how fast, how they speed up or slow down, and when they stay still.
terms.designer: The motion family: personality, duration ladder, easing curves, springs, enter and exit rules, reduced motion, and budgets per platform and device. Core durations sit between 100 and 300ms.
terms.engineer: DTCG duration, cubicBezier and transition tokens under motion.*. Springs have no DTCG type (issue #429), so they live in $extensions with a sampled CSS linear() fallback.

terms.plain: A few set times for how long each move takes, from instant to under a second.
terms.designer: Steps: instant 0, micro 100, short 150-200, medium 250-300, long 400-500, extra 700ms. Exits are 20-35% shorter; much past 500ms feels sluggish.
terms.engineer: DTCG duration tokens such as motion.duration.short = 150ms, on a ladder from .instant to .extra plus shorter exit steps. Figma variables import seconds only.
terms.example: A hover color changes in 100ms; full-screen dimming takes 700ms.

terms.plain: How a move speeds up or slows down, like a car easing to a stop instead of braking hard.
terms.designer: Four curves: standard for moves on screen, enter (decelerate) to arrive fast and settle, exit (accelerate) to get out of the way, linear only for spinners and progress.
terms.engineer: DTCG cubicBezier arrays: motion.easing.standard [0.2, 0, 0, 1], .enter [0, 0, 0, 1], .exit [0.3, 0, 1, 1], .linear. CSS gets cubic-bezier(); x stays within 0-1.
terms.example: A menu drops in fast and settles, then speeds away when closed.

terms.term: Enter and exit asymmetry and interruptibility
terms.plain: Things leave faster than they arrive, and if you act mid-move, the app responds at once.
terms.designer: Exits take about 70-80% of the entrance time and use an accelerate curve. Keep transitions interruptible, and never block input during a transition longer than about 100ms.
terms.engineer: Separate transition tokens, motion.transition.enter and motion.transition.exit. CSS transitions reverse from their current value while keyframe animations do not; SwiftUI springs retarget natively.
terms.example: Close a menu while it is still opening and it reverses at once.

terms.plain: Whether things move in a quick, calm way or a bouncy, fun way, and where fun is allowed.
terms.designer: Productive motion (short, strong ease-out, no overshoot) for about 90% of interactions; expressive motion for 1-3 hero moments per flow. Keep bounce at or below 0.2.
terms.engineer: No motion-scheme mode: the Energy dial scales durations and springs, unlike Material 3's MotionScheme (standard, expressive). Bounce at or below 0.2 equals a damping ratio of 0.8 or higher.
terms.example: Menus fade in quickly; only the success screen gets a small bounce.

terms.term: Motion by platform and device class
terms.plain: The phone runs its own screen changes, the brand styles small moves, and cars and watches move less.
terms.designer: The OS owns screen transitions, back and sheets; the brand owns how things inside a screen react. The motion budget shrinks as attention narrows, to little or none in cars.
terms.engineer: OS transitions (navigation, back, sheets) are not tokenized. Not generated yet: a motion context modifier mapping device classes, such as handheld full, wrist minimal, vehicle none, to duration multipliers.
terms.example: Back swipes use the phone's own slide; the brand animates only in-screen controls.

terms.plain: Moves that act like a real spring, slowing to a stop on their own.
terms.designer: Springs feel natural and keep their momentum when interrupted, unlike fixed curves. Use critically damped springs for UI transitions and a little bounce only for spatial hero motion.
terms.engineer: No DTCG spring type: store dampingRatio and stiffness in $extensions, derive duration and bounce for SwiftUI Spring(duration:bounce:), use Compose spring(), and pre-sample CSS linear().
terms.example: A sheet dragged halfway and let go springs back smoothly into place.

terms.plain: Feedback you feel or hear instead of see, like a small buzz or a soft click.
terms.designer: Non-visual feedback: haptic patterns and UI sounds (earcons). Used sparingly, they confirm actions and make the UI feel physical; overused, they annoy and feel cheap.
terms.engineer: No DTCG type for haptics or sound, and none generated: OpenDesigner records the haptics.intensity parameter and sends sounds and custom haptics to the H-sound and H-haptic hooks.
terms.example: A light tap on the wrist when a payment goes through.

terms.plain: A small set of buzzes the phone makes for things like a win, a warning, or flipping a switch.
terms.designer: About six semantic events (success, warning, error, selection, toggle, impact), used sparingly. Crisp, short haptics feel premium; long buzzy vibrations feel cheap. Standard controls already play their own.
terms.engineer: Not generated yet: string tokens such as haptic.feedback.success (proposed), mapped to iOS UIFeedbackGenerator .success and Android HapticFeedbackConstants.CONFIRM. Only haptics.intensity exists. Never store raw vibration durations.
terms.example: A crisp tick each time a picker wheel moves to the next item.

terms.plain: Whether the app makes little sounds when things happen, like a chime when a message is sent.
terms.designer: Silent by default on web and productivity apps. Earcons only for rare, meaningful events on mobile, games or spatial platforms, always with a mute option, never as the only signal.
terms.engineer: No DTCG type and none generated: sounds would be file references plus a volume (proposed), requested through hook H-sound. On iOS, the audio session category should respect the silent switch.
terms.example: A payment app plays one short sound on success and stays silent otherwise.

terms.plain: How round the corners are, and the lines that outline and split things on screen.
terms.designer: Corner radius (scale, personality, per-component roles, nesting, expressive shapes) plus borders, strokes and dividers. Radius is where systems diverge most, from square to pill; every 2025-2026 revision got rounder.
terms.engineer: Radius primitives are DTCG dimensions (radius.4 = 4px, radius.full), aliased by roles such as radius.control and radius.container. Strokes use border.width.* and color.border.*.
terms.example: A card with 12px corners and a thin gray outline.

terms.plain: How thick the outlines are, and when a thin line splits one part of the screen from the next.
terms.designer: Widths 1, 2, 4px: 1 by default, 2 for selected and focus, 4 for emphasis. Separate with space or a surface change before lines; lines suit dense data views.
terms.engineer: Dimension tokens border.width.1, .2 and .4, aliased by border.width.default, .selected and .emphasis; DTCG border composites bundle color, width and style. Width changes use inset box-shadow.
terms.example: A 2px outline marks the selected card while the others keep 1px.

terms.plain: Pill shapes and fun shapes like flowers, kept for a few spots where they count.
terms.designer: Pills read tappable and friendly. Expressive shapes and shape morphing add play; use them for avatars, loaders, image masks or FABs, and limit them to 1-3 signature uses.
terms.engineer: radius.full is a dimension token. Material 3 Expressive has 35 MaterialShapes as Compose RoundedPolygon objects; web needs SVG clip-path: path() or masks. Arbitrary shapes have no DTCG type.
terms.example: A flower-shaped photo frame for profile pictures in a playful Android app.

terms.plain: The kind of curve a corner has, and how a box inside a box gets corners that fit.
terms.designer: Circular arcs, or Apple's continuous corners, which ease into the edge. Nested shapes stay concentric: inner radius is outer radius minus padding, so the gap stays even.
terms.engineer: Inner radius is computed at generation, max(outer - padding, smallest step), and emitted as radius.nested. iOS uses .continuous; squircle-enhance adds CSS superellipse(1.35) corners at 1.22 times the radius.
terms.example: Card 16px, padding 8px, so the photo inside gets 8px corners.

terms.plain: How round the corners are all over the app, from sharp and serious to soft and friendly.
terms.designer: One dial (sharp, subtle, rounded, pill) sets every corner radius. Sharp reads technical, round reads friendly. Research favors subtle; OpenDesigner starts at 8px (Roundness 50). Logo curves inspire shapes.
terms.engineer: The Roundness dial picks, at generation, which primitive radius.control aliases, from a small step to {radius.full}; there is no shape-theme mode. Signature shapes are SVG assets.
terms.example: Sharp corners for a data tool, pill buttons for a playful consumer app.

terms.term: Radius scale and default control radius
terms.plain: A short list of how round corners can be, and the usual roundness for buttons.
terms.designer: Allowed corner radii plus the control default. Research default: 6px controls; OpenDesigner defaults to 8px controls, 12px containers at Roundness 50. Radius grows with size.
terms.engineer: DTCG dimension tokens: primitives radius.0 to radius.32 plus radius.full; roles radius.control, .container, .nested and .focus. CSS border-radius; Compose RoundedCornerShape; iOS continuous corners.
terms.example: Buttons with 8px corners inside cards with 12px corners.

terms.plain: Rules that give each kind of part its own roundness, small for tags and bigger for cards.
terms.designer: Named roles (detail, control, container, overlay, person) map the radius scale to component types. Radius steps up as elements get bigger, and full round is kept for avatars.
terms.engineer: Role tokens radius.detail, radius.control, radius.container, radius.overlay and radius.person alias radius primitives ($type dimension). Components use roles, never primitives; radius.person resolves to radius.full.
terms.example: Buttons 4-8px, cards 8-12px, avatars fully round.

terms.plain: How much room goes between and inside things, how big the parts are, and how tightly they pack.
terms.designer: The spacing scale and its named uses, the size ladders for controls and media, and density: how tightly the whole UI packs. Values converge; base unit and naming differ.
terms.engineer: DTCG dimension tokens in px or rem (dp and pt map to px): space.* steps, semantic space.inset.*, .stack.*, .inline.* and .section.*, size.control.*, size.icon.*, and density resolver contexts.
terms.example: The same 16px padding inside every card.

terms.plain: The one small step that every gap and size is counted in, like the marks on a ruler.
terms.designer: The unit every spacing and sizing value multiplies. Default: 4 as the grid, 8 as the rhythm. A pure 4 base suits dense tools; 8 suits marketing and content sites.
terms.engineer: Not a token: the unit, raw.spaceUnit (4 by default), is recorded in the space group's $extensions.opendesigner; the ladder multiplies it, so space.8 is 8px.
terms.example: Gaps of 4, 8, 16 and 24 pixels, all built from 4.

terms.plain: How much fits on the screen at once, packed tight or spread out, and who gets to choose.
terms.designer: How much content fits in an area and who controls it. Density changes layout, not only padding: body size, control height and row height.
terms.engineer: Dimension values per density resolver context (compact, comfortable, spacious), such as size.control.md at 32, 40 and 48. size.target.min sits outside the modifier and never changes.
terms.designer_says: density: how tightly the UI packs
terms.example: A spreadsheet packs rows tight; a shop page spreads things out.

terms.plain: How much to show at once depends on how far away you are, not how big the screen is.
terms.designer: Density follows viewing distance and input, not pixel count. A 65-inch TV is a far-away phone: phone-level density. Watches, cars and headsets stay sparse; desks can go compact.
terms.engineer: Not generated yet: density keyed to a context resolver modifier, not screen size, such as desk compact, handheld and leanback comfortable, wrist, vehicle and spatial sparse.
terms.example: A TV app shows about as much as a phone app, not a laptop.

terms.plain: Who picks how tight things are packed, the app or you, and which parts can pack tighter.
terms.designer: Who sets density (system, product or user) and which components get a compact mode. Consumer products stay comfortable; data tools offer a compact mode for tables, lists, menus and trees.
terms.engineer: The resolver's density modifier: compact, comfortable (default) or spacious. Compact drops insets, stacks and control heights about one scale step; size.target.min never changes.
terms.example: A 'Compact' option that makes table rows shorter so more fit.

terms.plain: Whether the whole app feels tight, cozy or roomy, and how big its text and buttons are.
terms.designer: The product-wide density personality: compact, comfortable or spacious, with the body size and control height that come with it. Comfortable suits apps, spacious suits marketing, compact suits data tools.
terms.engineer: The resolver's density modifier (compact, comfortable, spacious) swaps size.control.md and space.inset.*; the body size is set by the Density dial at generation, not per mode.
terms.example: An admin tool with 14px text and 32px buttons.

terms.plain: Whether the gaps get bigger when the window gets wider.
terms.designer: Only layout spacing (page margins, pane spacers, section gaps) grows with window size. Component spacing changes only with density, never with breakpoint, so controls feel the same everywhere.
terms.engineer: Not generated yet: layout tokens with breakpoint modes, such as layout.margin (proposed) = 16 / 24 / 24; component tokens get none. Native platforms use system layout guides and window size classes.
terms.example: Page margins grow from 16px in narrow windows to 24px in wider ones.

terms.plain: Lining up text lines and gaps on the same steps, like the lines in a notebook.
terms.designer: Line heights and vertical spacing snap to a 4px grid. Measure spacing from the text box instead of a strict baseline grid, and let layouts survive user text-spacing overrides.
terms.engineer: Line-height and section-spacing tokens sit on multiples of 4px on the spacing scale. On web, CSS text-box trimming is a progressive enhancement; text boxes never get fixed heights.
terms.example: Line heights such as 20px and 24px, both multiples of 4.

terms.plain: The short list of gap sizes you may use, so spacing never has to be guessed.
terms.designer: The ordered set of allowed gaps: about 15 steps from 0 to 96. 2px steps serve component internals; above 8px, aim for steps about 25% apart.
terms.engineer: Primitive dimension tokens named by pixel value, space.0 to space.96 (unit x 0 to 24), used through space.inset.*, .stack.*, .inline.* and .section.*. No negative steps.
terms.example: Padding of 16 and a gap of 8, never 15 or 7.

terms.plain: Names for what each gap is for, like room inside a button or space between cards.
terms.designer: Three named jobs: inset (padding inside a component), gap (between siblings in a stack or row), and layout (margins, pane spacers, sections). Insets can be square, squished or stretched.
terms.engineer: Semantic dimension aliases space.inset.*, .stack.*, .inline.* and .section.*, swapped per density. A squish inset would need separate block and inline tokens; DTCG 2025.10 has no padding composite.
terms.example: A pill button has less padding above and below than on its sides.

terms.plain: A few set sizes for buttons and icons, so things placed in a row line up.
terms.designer: Shared size ladders for interactive controls and for icons and avatars, so a button, input and icon placed side by side align on the same heights.
terms.engineer: Dimension tokens size.control.sm to .lg and size.icon.sm to .lg plus .default. Avatar sizes like size.avatar.xs (proposed) and component tokens are not generated yet.
terms.example: A 40px button and a 40px input side by side.

terms.plain: Small, medium and large heights that buttons, text boxes and menus share, so a row lines up.
terms.designer: Small, medium and large heights shared by buttons, inputs and selects: 32, 40, 48 for touch-inclusive products, 24, 32, 40 for pointer-first desktop tools. Don't mix sizes in one group.
terms.engineer: Dimension tokens size.control.sm, .md and .lg; component tokens like button.height.md (proposed) are not generated yet. Hit areas keep 44pt iOS and 48dp Android minimums.
terms.example: A search box and its button, both 40px tall.

terms.plain: A few set sizes for icons and the small round photos of people.
terms.designer: Fixed ladders so icons and avatars stay consistent: icons 16, 20, 24, 32; avatars 16 to 64 (Primer's set). Icon size equals the body line height minus 0-4px.
terms.engineer: Dimension tokens size.icon.sm = 16, .md = 20 and .lg = 24; avatar sizes like size.avatar.xs (proposed) are not generated yet. SF and Material Symbols can scale with text.
terms.example: A 16px icon in a small button, a 40px avatar beside a comment.

terms.plain: How roomy or packed things feel, and how gaps show what belongs together.
terms.designer: Airy or tight feel, set by the ratio of space inside a group to space between groups: at least 1:2, or 1:3 to 1:4 for airy brands.
terms.engineer: Semantic space.section.sm, .md and .lg set outer gaps and space.stack.* inner ones; engine.py validate errors when inner exceeds half the outer in any density.
terms.example: A label sits close to its field and far from the next one.

terms.plain: How the words in an app look: which fonts, what sizes, and how much space they get.
terms.designer: Typefaces, the type scale and its named roles, line height and spacing, text layout, and how text behaves across screens, zoom settings and non-Latin scripts.
terms.engineer: DTCG typography composite (fontFamily, fontSize, fontWeight, letterSpacing, lineHeight as a unitless multiplier), built from atomic fontFamily, fontWeight, dimension and number tokens. No slot for text case or paragraph spacing.
terms.example: Big bold headings, 16px body text for reading, small gray labels.

terms.plain: Making words in Hindi, Arabic and more look right, with backup fonts and room to fit.
terms.designer: Scripts to cover, a fallback stack for each, and script tweaks: taller line height for Indic and CJK, no italics or all caps outside Latin, right-to-left direction.
terms.engineer: Per-locale fontFamily fallback arrays, such as font.family.text for hi-IN, are not generated yet; the CSS export sets line heights for listed scripts through :lang() rules.
terms.example: Hindi text falls back to Noto Sans Devanagari with a taller line height.

terms.plain: Gaps between lines, letters and blocks of text, and how thick the letters are.
terms.designer: Line height near 1.5 for 12-16px, tighter as text grows; letter spacing 0 at body, negative on big headings; three weights; paragraph spacing about one body size.
terms.engineer: Typography composite: lineHeight is a unitless multiplier, letterSpacing a px or rem dimension, fontWeight 1-1000 or aliases like semi-bold. Paragraph spacing has no slot; use a separate dimension token.
terms.example: 16px body text with a 24px line height and no extra letter spacing.

terms.plain: Giving each digit the same width, so rows of prices line up neatly.
terms.designer: Proportional lining figures in running text, tabular lining figures in tables and live-updating numbers so digits line up and do not jump. Native digits serve other scripts.
terms.engineer: No DTCG slot for font features; store $extensions such as fontFeatureSettings: 'tnum', or emit component CSS font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums lining-nums.
terms.example: A countdown timer whose digits stay put as they change.

terms.plain: How text size changes on phones, watches and TVs, so it looks right from where you sit.
terms.designer: Body text stays fixed; display styles may go fluid on web. Farther screens need bigger numbers: body is 17pt on phone, 29pt on TV.
terms.engineer: DTCG has no fluid value like clamp(), so responsive type needs modes per breakpoint (not generated yet). Units: pt on Apple, sp on Android, epx on Windows, rem on web.
terms.example: Body text is 17 points on iPhone and 29 points on Apple TV.

terms.plain: Set text styles for each job, like big titles, reading text and small button words.
terms.designer: Named styles by job (display, headline, title, body, label, code), most in large, medium and small, with one emphasized weight per style. Emphasis uses weight first, color second.
terms.engineer: Typography composites by job and size, such as text.body.md, over primitives such as font.size.14 and font.weight.body. Emphasized variants are not generated yet.
terms.designer_says: type styles: display, headline, body, label
terms.example: Headline Large for a page title, Body Medium for paragraphs, Label Small for tags.

terms.plain: The fixed list of text sizes an app may use, from tiny labels to big headings.
terms.designer: Body size and the ratio that generates the rest. Body runs 14px for tools, 16px for reading; ratios run 1.125-1.2 for dense apps, 1.333+ for editorial.
terms.engineer: Primitive dimension tokens named by pixel size, such as font.size.14, from round(base x ratio^n); base and ratio sit in the group's $extensions.opendesigner.
terms.designer_says: type scale: base size and ratio
terms.example: Every heading picks from the same few sizes instead of a random one.

terms.plain: When you turn up text size in settings, the app still fits and reads well.
terms.designer: Support the user's text-size setting: Dynamic Type up to AX5, Android font scale to 200%, browser zoom to 200%. Containers grow with text, and layouts survive user text-spacing overrides.
terms.engineer: Text tokens use scalable units: rem on web, sp on Android, UIFont.TextStyle on iOS. Never put sp in spacing tokens; no text container gets a fixed height.
terms.example: At the largest text setting, a button grows taller instead of cutting off its label.

terms.plain: How long lines of text get, which side they line up on, and what happens when words don't fit.
terms.designer: Keep prose near 65-70 characters per line (35-40 for CJK). Default to start alignment and sentence case; wrap first, then ellipsis with access to the full text.
terms.engineer: No DTCG type for measure, case or truncation. DTCG dimensions allow only px and rem, so size.measure.prose (proposed) would keep 65ch in $extensions; casing stays in CSS.
terms.example: A help article capped at about 70 characters per line.

terms.plain: The style of letters an app uses, like the font you pick for a school report.
terms.designer: Which font families the system uses and why: where they come from, the personality they project, how many there are, their variable axes, and how they load.
terms.engineer: DTCG fontFamily tokens, a string or fallback array: font.family.text for UI and body, font.family.display for headings (aliases text by default) and font.family.mono.
terms.example: Inter for the whole app, plus a code font for snippets.

terms.plain: One font that can slide from thin to bold and reshape its letters for small or big text.
terms.designer: Variable fonts expose axes such as weight, optical size and grade. Default: a font with wght and opsz, with optical size tied to font size.
terms.engineer: DTCG fontWeight takes 1-1000; the typography composite has no slot for opsz, GRAD or wdth, so they live in $extensions. CSS: font-optical-sizing: auto.
terms.example: One font file covers regular, semibold and bold.

terms.plain: The rules for using a font, and how it shows up fast without text jumping.
terms.designer: How fonts are licensed, packaged and loaded, and what that costs in speed. Each web family adds download time, so budget two families and show a fallback first.
terms.engineer: Not tokenized beyond the fontFamily fallback array; @font-face CSS is not generated yet. Default advice: WOFF2, one variable file per family, font-display: swap, a metric-adjusted fallback and per-script subsets.
terms.example: Text appears at once in a system font, then swaps to the brand font.

terms.plain: How many fonts an app uses, which ones pair well, and a font for code.
terms.designer: Default to one UI family plus one monospace, adding a serif or display face only for marketing. Pair siblings that share x-height, contrast and width; tabular figures handle data.
terms.engineer: font.family.text, .display and .mono ($type fontFamily); the composites text.code.sm and text.code.md use mono. Numeric cells get font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums.
terms.example: One sans-serif for the app and a monospace font for code samples.

terms.plain: The mood a font's letter shapes give, such as friendly, serious, new or old.
terms.designer: The type class (neo-grotesque, humanist, geometric, serif, rounded) chosen from brand adjectives, then vetoed if letters get confused at 12-14px or scripts are missing.
terms.engineer: Not a token itself: it guides the value of font.family.*. The engine records the param type.faceSuggestion.classification, such as neutral-sans, in opendesigner.meta.json to drive recommendations.
terms.designer_says: type class, like neo-grotesque or humanist
terms.example: A rounded font feels playful; a serif leans toward heritage.

terms.plain: Whether an app uses the font that came with your device, a free font, or its own.
terms.designer: System stack, open neutral face (Inter, Roboto) or custom brand face, and which roles get which on each platform. Common split: brand for display and headlines, system for body.
terms.engineer: font.family.text holds one fallback array, such as system-ui, -apple-system, Segoe UI, Roboto, so each platform picks its system face. Apple's SF is system-only; custom faces must be bundled.
terms.designer_says: system, open or custom brand face
terms.example: SF Pro on iPhone, Roboto on Android, the brand font for headlines.

terms.plain: Saved, named choices, like a brand blue, that design apps and code can share.
terms.designer: Named values that store every foundation decision, such as color.bg.accent instead of a hex code. Change one token and every design and screen that uses it follows.
terms.engineer: The data layer: tiers, naming, coverage, types, modes, themes and delivery. engine.py generate writes DTCG 2025.10 files plus a Resolver; springs and P3 colors ride in $extensions.opendesigner.

terms.plain: Which choices get a saved name, and which stay as one-off numbers.
terms.designer: Which properties become tokens. Default: everything Figma variables can bind and Check designs can lint, plus motion and focus; one-off illustration values stay out.
